bloecke.md:
When you buy a condominium unit, you acquire three things at once: ownership of the unit itself, an undivided percentage interest in the common elements and a mandatory membership in the condominium association. The association is usually a nonprofit corporation run by a board of directors that the owners elect. It is governed by state law, by the declaration recorded in the county land records and by its bylaws and rules. It enters into contracts, collects assessments, holds the reserves, sues and can be sued. You take part in management through your vote, not through a right to decide alone.

Where the unit ends and the common elements begin is defined in the declaration and often differs from what owners expect. Roof, exterior walls, structural elements, hallways, elevators and building systems are usually common elements. Balconies, assigned parking spaces and storage lockers are often limited common elements: they are reserved for one unit, but the association may still decide on their repair and charge the costs. Whether windows, sliding doors or the pipes inside the walls belong to the unit or to the association differs from building to building, and with it who pays when they fail.

## Declaration, bylaws and rules

The **declaration** (in planned communities usually called CC&Rs, covenants, conditions and restrictions) creates the condominium, describes the units and the common elements and assigns each unit its allocated interests: its share of the common elements, of the common expenses and of the votes. These shares are usually based on unit size or on the original price ratio; sometimes they are equal per unit. The plat and floor plans recorded with it show which parking space or storage room belongs to the unit and which is only assigned to it.

The **bylaws** govern the association's internal procedures, such as board elections, meetings, quorum and officers. The **rules and regulations** cover daily life, from pets to renovations; the board can usually change them without a vote of the owners. Changing the declaration, by contrast, typically requires a supermajority of owners, often two thirds or three quarters, as set in the declaration or in state law. Recorded covenants bind every later buyer. They frequently restrict renting: minimum lease terms, bans on short-term rentals or a cap on the number of units that may be rented. For an investor, such a clause can decide whether the purchase makes sense at all.

bloecke.md:
## Dues, budget and assessments

The board adopts an annual budget, and each owner's monthly dues are the budget multiplied by the unit's share of the common expenses. In most states, owners do not adopt the budget themselves; they elect the board that does. Some states give owners the right to reject a budget at a meeting or require a vote of the owners above a certain increase.

Low dues are not an argument for buying, because they usually mean that the association sets little aside or defers maintenance. Insurance has become the fastest-rising item in many buildings, especially in states exposed to hurricanes and wildfires. The master policy covers the structure; owners need their own HO-6 policy for the interior, their belongings, liability and their share of assessments after an uninsured loss. For a landlord, regular dues are deductible on Schedule E; a special assessment for an improvement, by contrast, must be capitalized and depreciated. Before buying, ask for the current budget, the most recent financial statements and the year-to-date figures. They show whether income covers spending or whether a deficit is building up.

bloecke.titel: Three key figures on the association
bloecke.md: The meaningful figures are the monthly dues relative to the size of the unit, the reserve balance relative to what the reserve study says it should be (percent funded) and the share of owners who are 60 days or more behind on their dues. The first two can be found in the budget, the financial statements and the reserve study; you have to ask for the third. Dues that some owners do not pay are ultimately borne by the others.

## Reserves and the reserve study

Proper management includes saving for components that wear out on a predictable schedule: roof, elevators, facade, paving, boilers. A **reserve study** lists these components with their remaining useful life and replacement cost and derives the annual contribution needed. Its key figure is the percent funded: the reserve balance divided by the amount that should have been accumulated by now, given the age of the components.

There is no nationwide rule on how much an association must set aside. Some states require reserve studies; California, for example, requires a visual inspection of the major components at least every three years. After the collapse of the Champlain Towers South condominium in Surfside, Florida, in June 2021, which killed 98 people, Florida introduced mandatory milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condo buildings of three stories or more, and associations can no longer vote to waive reserves for structural components. Many associations there faced sharp increases in dues and large special assessments. Mortgage investors also look at reserves: for a condo project to be eligible for loans sold to Fannie Mae, the budget generally has to allocate at least 10% to reserves, and no more than 15% of the units may be 60 or more days behind on their dues.

serien.name: Special assessment per unit in dollars

bloecke.md: Reserves lose value as construction costs rise. A reserve that would have covered a roof ten years ago may now cover only part of it. The association raises the missing amount through a special assessment, a one-time charge on top of the regular dues. Depending on the declaration and state law, the board can impose it alone or needs a vote of the owners. In California, for example, the board may impose special assessments of up to 5% of the year's budgeted gross expenses without a vote of the members; emergencies are exempt from this limit. Associations can also take out a bank loan and repay it through higher dues over several years.

bloecke.formel: Special assessment per unit = (Project cost − Withdrawal from reserves) × Share of common expenses
bloecke.erklaerung: The same allocation applies as for the regular dues unless the declaration provides otherwise.

bloecke.beispiel: Illustrative calculation: facade and balcony repairs cost $1,800,000, of which $500,000 comes from reserves, leaving $1,300,000. A unit with a 1.85% share pays $1,300,000 × 0.0185 = $24,050.

bloecke.md: As a rule, a special assessment is owed by whoever owns the unit when an installment falls due, not by whoever owned it when it was approved. If an assessment is approved in March and the second installment is due in October, a buyer who closed in August pays it unless the purchase contract says otherwise. Many states require the seller or the association to provide a resale certificate or estoppel letter before closing that lists the dues, unpaid amounts and approved special assessments. Ask also about assessments that are being discussed but not yet approved, and read the latest board minutes. Unpaid dues and assessments are secured by a lien on the unit, and the association can foreclose on it. In a number of states, part of that lien even takes priority over the first mortgage.

## Owners' meetings and voting

The association holds at least an annual meeting, mainly to elect the board. Notice periods, quorum and voting rules come from state law and the bylaws. Quorums are often low, and some states allow them to be lowered further if a meeting fails for lack of a quorum. Owners who neither attend nor send a proxy or absentee ballot leave the decision to those present. Most decisions, including the budget, contracts, repairs and often special assessments within the limits described above, are made by the board and not by the owners. Directors owe the association a fiduciary duty, but courts generally defer to their decisions as long as they are made in good faith and on an informed basis (business judgment rule).

Owners vote directly on electing and removing directors, on amending the declaration and, depending on state law and the documents, on large assessments or borrowing. Whether an owner can install a satellite dish, solar panels or an EV charger against the association's will depends on federal and state law. The FCC's Over-the-Air Reception Devices rule protects small antennas and dishes in areas the owner uses exclusively, and several states limit an association's power to ban solar panels or EV chargers.

bloecke.md:
## Management company and board

Most larger associations hire a professional management company that collects dues, pays bills, obtains bids and prepares the budget. Some states, Florida for example, require community association managers to be licensed. The management contract is concluded by the board; its term, fee and termination rights are set in the contract, not in the law. Self-managed associations rely on volunteer directors. That can be inexpensive and well run, or it can mean that nobody keeps the records.

In a co-op, the board has more power than in a condo. It approves or rejects buyers and subtenants after reviewing a board package with tax returns, bank statements and references, and many co-ops require a minimum down payment and liquid assets left over after closing. Sublet rules are often strict, and some co-ops charge a flip tax on sales, a fee paid to the corporation, usually by the seller.

bloecke.md: First read the minutes of the last three years in chronological order and note every postponed repair and every engineering report mentioned. Then take the reserve balance from the latest financial statement, divide it by the number of units and compare it with the reserve study's recommended balance and with the components due in the next ten years. If a 40-year-old building has a reserve of a few thousand dollars per unit and a roof or facade project ahead, a special assessment is almost certain; only the timing is open. Next, ask the manager for the share of owners behind on dues and for the terms of the latest insurance renewal, and check whether your lender considers the project eligible (warrantable). A project that is not makes financing harder and a later sale slower.

Owner-occupants cannot deduct condo or HOA dues. Condo owners deduct their own property tax and mortgage interest as itemized deductions. Co-op shareholders can deduct their proportionate share of the corporation's mortgage interest and real estate taxes under 26 U.S.C. § 216; the co-op reports the amounts each year. Real estate taxes count toward the cap on the deduction for state and local taxes, which is $40,400 for 2026 and is reduced for incomes above $505,000. Landlords deduct regular dues as rental expenses; special assessments for improvements are capitalized.

Building rules increasingly affect associations as well. New York City's Local Law 97 sets emissions limits for most buildings over 25,000 square feet, with fines for exceeding them, so the boards of large condos and co-ops must plan for new boilers and other upgrades. Several other cities have similar building performance standards. The federal tax credits for energy-efficient home improvements and residential solar ended for most expenditures after 2025. As with any large project, the investment is decided by the board and paid through dues, reserves or a special assessment.

mitnehmen: With a condo, you acquire at the same time a unit, a percentage interest in the common elements, a mandatory membership in the association and the obligation to abide by its recorded covenants and past decisions.
Low dues usually mean postponed costs; the percent funded from the reserve study shows whether the association saves enough for the components it will have to replace.
In most states, the board and not the owners adopts the budget and decides most matters, and a special assessment is owed by whoever owns the unit when an installment falls due.
Unpaid dues are secured by a lien that the association can foreclose, in some states with partial priority over the first mortgage.
Co-ops differ fundamentally: you buy shares and a lease, the board approves buyers, and the monthly maintenance includes the building's property tax and mortgage interest.

begriffe.text: Mandatory association of all unit owners, usually a nonprofit corporation run by an elected board. It manages the common elements, collects dues, holds the reserves and can place a lien on units with unpaid assessments.

Recorded document that creates a condominium or planned community, describes units and common elements and assigns each unit its share of the common elements, expenses and votes. Its covenants, for example on renting, bind every later buyer.

Analysis of the components an association must repair or replace, with their remaining useful life and cost. Its key figure, the percent funded, compares the actual reserve balance with the balance that should have been accumulated.
One-time charge on top of the regular dues when reserves do not cover a project. It is allocated like the regular dues and owed by whoever owns the unit when an installment falls due.

Statement by the association before a sale that lists the dues, amounts owed, approved special assessments and often pending litigation. Many states require it; the buyer can rely on the amounts stated.

Long-term lease that a co-op corporation grants to each shareholder for a specific apartment. Together with the shares, it is what a co-op buyer acquires; the board can restrict subletting and must approve transfers.
